notes.1a: A few candidates misread $277.20 as $227.20 in this part and lost an accuracy mark.
notes.1ai: Nearly all candidates gave the correct answer for this part. A few rounded the answer to £34.7 -the answer was exactly £34.65 and in the case of money it should be left and not rounded.
notes.1aii: This again was answered correctly by most candidates with a few rounding to 3 s.f. as in part (i) .
notes.1aiii: The majority of the candidates showed their working and obtained the correct answer, Some worked out 95% of $277.20 rather than realising that the $277.20 was 105% of the previous week’s total.
notes.1bi: Ratios were dealt with correctly by nearly all candidates.
notes.1bii: This part was yet again mostly correct. The common error was to calculate × $ 2200 , rather than dividing by .
notes.2ai: Y was usually correct. A few reflected in the y-axis and a very small number of candidates made other errors.
notes.2aii: Again mostly correct or a correct rotation of their Y . A few candidates rotated anticlockwise rather than clockwise.
notes.2aiii: The descriptions after fully correct answers in parts (i) and (ii) were mostly correct. A few thought the reflection line was y = x . Those who made errors with the images Y and Z , were less successful with their descriptions. Some missed out parts of their description while others created a Z image which was impossible to transform onto X using a single transformation. Very few candidates tried to give a combination of transformations.
notes.2bi: Most enlargements were correct though a few candidates used the wrong centre or enlarged by scale factor - .
notes.2bii: Although a reasonable proportion of candidates found the correct matrix, many computed the coordinates and wrote those in their matrix.
notes.2ci: This proved to be the most difficult part of the question for many candidates and a large number did not attempt it. Answers were usually in the correct region of the grid but errors with several plotted points were common. Some used the y-axis or y = 4 as the invariant line.
notes.2cii: This was a challenging part with few correct matrices seen. Some attempted to form a matrix equation. However a few candidates gave a correct answer without attempting the transformation or after a wrong transformation. ⎛ 0 . 5 0 ⎞ ⎛ 1 − 1 ⎞ ⎜ ⎟ ⎜ ⎟
notes.3a: The difference between the two areas was used correctly by most candidates to show that x -10x – 24 = 0. Those who expanded (x+5) usually did so correctly. The most common errors were to start with the difference the wrong way round or to miss the =0 at some stage. A few started with x -10x + 24 =0 and tried to factorise it.
notes.3b: This was well answered by the majority of candidates - even those who had not been successful in part (a) . Most factorised correctly but a few used the formula, which was fine if they used it correctly. Some failed to relate the equation back to the initial problem so incorrectly included -2 as a possible value of x.
notes.3c: This part caused more problems than the rest of the question. Some found the correct angle but it was very rare to see the most efficient method being used. There were numerous incorrect answers of 26.6° where candidates did not recognise that they needed to double this angle. Most candidates tended to use a combination of Pythagoras’ theorem, sine rule and cosine rule. This often resulted in errors being made.
notes.4a: Most candidates realised that use of the cosine rule was necessary and cos A = 19/96 was usually seen. This was often immediately followed by A = 78.6 without first showing the more accurate value of 78.58…which was required as evidence of a value rounding to 78.6. (b ) (i) The answers to this part were mostly correct. A few thought the required angle was BMO and gave o o an answer of 90 . Others gave angle BOC , having 157.2 as their answer.
notes.4aii: Most used triangle BOM and the sine of angle BOM, but others used triangle BOC and the sine rule. As in part (a) , some candidates did not show all the required working and only gave r = 4.5/sin 78.6 → r = 4.59 which earned just M2 or sin 78.6 = 4.5/r → r = 4.59 which earned M1 or even r = 4.5/sin BOM → r = 4.59 which earned zero.
notes.4c: Many candidates gained full marks. Various methods of finding the area of the triangle were used, including long methods and these were often successful. Some firstly calculated the perpendicular 2 2 2 2 2 height of the triangle by combining two simultaneous equations e.g. 8 = (9-x) + h and 6 = x + h . There were some cases of premature rounding which resulted in the final answer being outside the acceptable range of answers.
notes.5a: The table was generally completed correctly. The most common error was to give f(x) = 9.1 rather than 9.11 for x-= -3 and +3. A few gave f(x) =1 rather than 2 for x= -1 and +1.
notes.5b: Plotting was mostly good but the scale on the y-axis caught out a number of candidates– mainly at 4.25 which was sometimes plotted at 4.5 and was costly if all 4 points were wrong. Only a handful did not attempt a smooth curve though a few joined with straight lines or missed points by too large a distance. Encouragingly, hardly anyone joined the two branches.
notes.5ci: The majority of candidates correctly wrote down x = 0. As this required a line equation “y-axis” was not good enough. y=0 was a common wrong answer, and a few candidates did not attempt this.
notes.5cii: A good proportion drew an acceptable tangent but some drew a line from the point to the origin thus making a chord, and a few drew the tangent at 1.5. Although many got the correct gradient, it was quite common to lose the negative sign or to make a slip in calculation or with reading off values from their graph.
notes.5ciii: The majority of candidates gained some credit but some values were slightly outside the acceptable ranges.
notes.5civ: The more able recognised the need to draw y= 2x accurately and found the two values. Many did not draw anything but put answers of 1 and -1 thus scoring one mark.
notes.9ai: The correct answer of 81 was obtained by nearly all candidates. A few worked out f(2) x g(2) and gave an answer of 112.
notes.9aii: As with part (i) most candidates again gave the correct answer. There were no common wrong answers (b) The correct inverse was found in most cases. A small number of candidates gave an answer of x + 1 (c) The correct value in its simplest form was normally found. A few tried to further simplify the correct answer and some left the answer as 3(x+2) +1.
notes.9d: There was very good use of the quadratic formula by most candidates and those who used the method of completing the square were also normally successful. The main error was to give the answers to the wrong degree of accuracy. It was required to 2 decimal places. A common error was to give the answers to 3 s.f rather than 2 d.p. i.e. -0.382 and -2.62 which lost one mark. There were also some who left the answer in surd form. There were very few cases of answers without working. x − 1
